questions.q: What is the difference between reproducibility and replicability, as defined in this lesson?
options: Reproducibility uses the original code/data to get the same result; replicability uses an independent implementation to get a consistent result
They are two names for exactly the same test
Reproducibility only applies to simulators; replicability only applies to hardware
Replicability means publishing in a peer-reviewed journal
questions.explain: The lesson defines reproducibility as re-running the original pipeline for the same result, and replicability as an independent implementation of the same method producing a consistent result -- a result can pass one and fail the other.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a reproduction attempt on real quantum hardware is 'automatically also partially a robustness check'?
options: Because real quantum hardware's noise characteristics change over time, so you're never running on the exact device-state the original authors used
Because hardware reproduction attempts always use a different algorithm
Because real hardware never produces any measurable output
Because robustness checks require a noiseless simulator by definition
questions.explain: The lesson explains that quantum hardware is not a fixed instrument -- its noise characteristics drift over time -- so any hardware reproduction attempt is inherently also testing whether the result holds under a changed device state, which is what a robustness check measures.

questions.q: Which reproduction target does this course's reproduction lab (Lesson 10) aim for, per this lesson?
options: Replicability -- writing your own independent implementation of the described method
Exact reproducibility using the original authors' exact code and data
Robustness across ten or more different hardware devices
None of these -- the lab does not target any specific goal
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that the reproduction lab targets replicability: writing your own implementation rather than just re-running someone else's script.

questions.q: According to the lesson's realistic tiering of reproduction goals, which is the LEAST demanding, legitimate target?
options: Reproducing the qualitative pattern (e.g., the direction of an effect) without matching exact numbers
Reproducing the exact reported numbers to the decimal point
Reproducing results on ten independent hardware devices simultaneously
Publishing a peer-reviewed rebuttal of the original paper
questions.explain: The lesson lists three tiers in order of difficulty, with reproducing the qualitative pattern (direction of effect, without exact numbers) as the easiest and a completely legitimate target for a capstone-level attempt.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a FAILED reproduction attempt is not a wasted exercise?
options: It forces identification of exactly which assumption, parameter, or environmental factor explains the gap, which is itself a valuable, sometimes publishable finding
Because failed reproductions are always due to the original paper being fraudulent
Because failed attempts require no further analysis or write-up
Because reproduction attempts never actually fail in quantum computing
questions.explain: The lesson states that failed reproductions are often the most instructive outcome, and that some of the most useful papers in the field are themselves reproduction attempts showing a prior claim didn't hold under different conditions -- a real contribution, covered further in Lesson 9.
